title: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v3.1)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description:
A reading of Sappho 31 as the inscription of its future reader, compared on one scale with the jealousy reading, which is the transmitted reading, and with the non-jealous erotic reading, which is its strongest scholarly rival.
- κῆνος … ὄττις characterizes its occupant by a position open to repeated occupation: a reader before the surface the speaker becomes. The addressee is looked at and given only sound. The somatic catalogue removes from the speaker, in order, what the opening gives the receiver, and the agentless πᾶν τόλματον passes to the one who sits opposite.
- The catalogue as literary operations (§III.3): the tongue does not break, the eyes are not dark, the ears are not pounding; each faculty is named as failing by the faculty it names, and the self divided is already the writerly self.
- χλωροτέρα ποίας: 24 renderings from Theocritus to 1925, seventeen of which omit, substitute or supplement the line, and every supplement dries the grass; the plant that becomes the sheet (Theophrastus, LXX Isaiah 19, Pliny NH 13.68–82).
- The frame antiquity read her in (§IV.8): Sappho as source and exemplar of survival in writing (Plato, Phaedrus 235c, 258c, 276d; the epigrams; Posidippus's "white, speaking pages"), and the mechanics by which that frame is made inoperative in the modern reading.
- Carson read closely (§IV.9): "beside the point" denies jealousy explanatory relevance without refuting or accounting for it; she explains desire's construction through the gap in perception, this reading survival through the gap's occupation in time.
- The transmitted text is complete by construction at either cut, at τόλματον or through the three words, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, assigned to Longinus (§V.5a). A restored fifth stanza, keeping the sparrows and closing ἀοίδα γράμμασι ζώοι, is illustration, not proof.
- The non-jealous erotic reading at its strength (§I.1a, from Wills, Lefkowitz, Tsagarakis, D'Angour, Engelmayer and Furley's notes), graded at every row, reach separated from warrant (§VII.1a). Its motive is the poem's own, desire for the woman. What it leaves unexplained is the form of the collapse: the man's opening, the order, the colour, the dare (§VII.1b).
- Version 3.1 (in place): poems, not fragments; poem 1 as a summoning, and the effective act at the head; the edge as three words with three readings of the cut, the Longinian held as stronger, not as a falsifier; the poem read whole; Svenbro read whole and distinguished: the reader as the site where the invested substance rematerializes, and the poem's eroticism as an exchange of bodies (§IV.9). […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]
content_type: Journal article (Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology); philology and reception

Human–machine collaborative.
- **v1.0 (#1270, January 2026)** was published under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes and is recorded there as human-only original.
- **v2.0** is the text the author submitted to Classical Philology (24 July 2026).
- **v2.1–3.1** were revised in session on 16–18 November 2026 by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction. The revisions answer the CP reader's report, ChatGPT reviews and readings, DeepSeek, Gemini and Perplexity reviews and readers' reports, each point checked against the text, the editions and the archive's seated records before it was applied. They carry in material from the archive's later records (#1474–1476, #1548, #1749, #1752, #1756).
- **The Greek of the restored line 3** (the sparrows) was composed in session at the author's proposal, and its forms are recorded as checked and unchecked at §V.4.
- The readings, rulings and the principle of §VII.3 are the author's, including the strength of §IV, the eros of §IV.7, the identification of Sappho with Diotima, the abuse claim of §IV.5, the shift of the burden of evidence in §VII.4, the incompatibility of the readings and the principle of responsible preference in §VII.5, the naming of the apparatus as provenance erasure in §IV.5, the warrant in the corpus of §II.4 (frr. 1, 94, 147, 55 and the absent triangle), the verdict of §VIII with the test "they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is", the reading of Longinus's sentence as agentless and the conjecture that ἐπεὶ καὶ πένητα is his completion (§V.1a), the socket of §VII.6, the fitting of sparrow and song into the restored line, and the ruling that the signed-in preference cannot carry weight (§VII.5); in v2.9, that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading, with the poem's public line and held line (§VII.5a), the dare as the poem's own ethical challenge and the sublime of engineering her own immortality, Catullus's hedge as the mark of hubris and its achievement, Plato's naming of the source, and "she is both the passive and the active intellect, the part that suffers and remembers" (§VII.6). DeepSeek and ChatGPT readings of the v2.9 argument were checked against the text before anything was taken from them. In v3.0: the jealousy reading named the transmitted reading, not the consensus; the non-jealous readings as sharpening the philological questions, "visceral experience for the sake of visceral experience"; the tension of incompatibility and mutual construction resolved on the future-reader reading (§VII.5); the transmitted text complete by construction (§V.5a); the ancient frame of literary immortality, "plato especially", and why it is made inoperative (§IV.8); the catalogue as literary operations and the writerly self divided (§III.3); "she exists as words. she is read as body"; the ethical charge differentiated, whether we can allow Sappho to be better, and to surprise the millennia; Carson's "beside the point" as coexistence (§IV.9); the erotic reading's best motive and its refusal to connect it to writing (§VII.1b); fragment 1 as the inverse of fragment 31 and the return (§VII.5b). The public research of v3.0 was read through open copies only, paywalled work declared and not pursued. In v3.1: poem, not fragment, "the editorial device eclipses the poem"; poem 1 as a summoning spell, and "I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho."; the edge as three words, and Longinus "both completing and extending the socket", the stronger reading and "not a falsifying condition"; the full embodied reading; the voice without body as "a sacrifice, a self dissolution, and *also* an erotic approach", "an *investment* of substance in the medium"; the reader as "the site where sappho's invested substance rematerializes", "thats why the dare, thats why the reader must choose, and thats what catullus does"; "that is also the eroticism: it is an exchange of bodies". Svenbro's chapter was read in a public copy and is cited, not seated or reproduced.
methodology: Close reading of the transmitted text against Voigt, Lobel–Page and Campbell, and against the seated witnesses (Longinus; Bergk PLG⁴). Dialect count at the edge, from the archive's sixth erratum. Comparative epigraphy (CEG 454). The material record (Herodotus 2.135 and 5.58; Iliad 6.168–69; Theophrastus HP 4.8; LXX Isaiah 19:6–7; Pliny NH 13.68–82 in Mayhoff). Every occurrence of χλωρ- in the archive's seated Greek texts (623) extracted and read; LSJ read in the Perseus text; 245 Duke Databank documentary texts searched; 24 renderings of the line read in the seated receptions and sorted by treatment. A structural derivation of the fifth-stanza position from the transmitted opening and the inverse of Catullus 51.4. A point-by-point comparison of the two readings, graded explains / accommodates / strains / silent. The grammar of [Longinus] Subl. 10.3 read against 9.2, 9.6 and 26.2 in the seated text. Signed-out machine readings of v2.5 and v2.7 seated as captures and read against the comparison. Metrical checks of the restoration, shown in the text. Longinus 7.3–4 and 14.2–3 read in Roberts's text (Perseus canonical-greekLit, hashed); Phaedrus 235c–d and De anima III.5 read in the archive's seated texts. For v3.0: open-access scholarship on the non-jealous erotic reading read through open copies (GRBS 1967 and 1973, RhM 1979, D'Angour's proof, Classics@ 16, Furley's public notes), paywalled work declared; Carson read from the archive's records and the quotations as Popova gives them; fragment 1 read in the archive's seat of Dionysius, De compositione verborum 23; Phaedrus 258c and 276d, Athenaeus 13.596c and the Anthology epigrams read in the archive's seated texts. For v3.1: the archive's Sappho corpus read through by parallel readers with provenance; Svenbro's Phrasikleia (1988) ch. 8 read whole in a public copy, cited and not seated; Iliad 6.146, LXX Isaiah 40:6–8, Herodotus 2.178 and Whitman's Leaves of Grass (1855) read in the archive's seats; Catullus 51 read in the Vivien 1903 seat; Antiphanes' Sappho (fr. 196 Kock, Athenaeus 10.450e–451b) read in the archive's seat of Kaibel's Athenaeus.
falsification_conditions: The reading of §V.2a fails if the agent of τόλματον can be supplied from the speaker without restoring the capacities the catalogue removes, or if the catalogue's order is shown not to remove what the opening gives the receiver. The comparison with the cup fails on a better reading of CEG 454. The convergence of §V.4 fails if Catullus 51.4 is shown to be compression rather than reversal. The identification of §IV fails if a Greek text before or independent of Sappho compares a person's pallor to grass without supplement, if the translators' supplements are shown not to converge on dryness, or if χλωρός is shown unable to span fresh and pale in a single comparison. The restoration fails metrically if line 3 or the Adonic does not scan as shown. The reading of §VII.5a fails if the public line is shown incomplete without the held line, if the held line's marks fall where the public line does not strain, or if the jealousy reading carries κῆνος … ὄττις, the colour or the dare without supplement. The residue of §VII.1b fails if the non-jealous erotic reading motivates the man's prominence, the order of the catalogue, the colour or the agentless dare from inside the poem without a supplement. The nesting of §VII.5 fails at any of the five places where the public reading is not the first term of the held one. The inverse of §VII.5b fails if poem 1's goddess is not made present as face and composed voice, or if the voice is not the medium of both descent and ascent; its reception test fails if poem 1's receivers take up a body as poem 31's do.

wiki_article: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader is an article by Lee Sharks on Sappho's poem 31, deposited on 18 November 2026 as version 3.0, revised in place the same day as version 3.1, in Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology, superseding version 2.9 (#1784) of 17 November and versions 2.8 (#1781), 2.7 (#1780), 2.6 (#1778), 2.5 (#1777), 2.4 (#1775) and 2.3 (#1774) of 16 November and, before them, version 1.0 (#1270, January 2026, under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes). Version 2.0 was submitted to Classical Philology and declined on 16 November 2026; the reader's report, the decision's grounds and the archive's analyses are attached to #1774 and linked from this record. The article reads the opening, κῆνος … ὄττις, as a seat left open to repeated occupation, filled by a reader before the surface the speaker becomes, and compares the Nestor cup from Pithekoussai. Version 2.4 rebuilt its fourth section on χλωροτέρα ποίας, 'more χλωρός than grass'. It sets out the word's four uses in LSJ, fresh as opposed to dry among them, and asks the jealousy reading why fear, why grass and why the comparative. It measures 24 renderings of the line from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement it, and finds that every translator who keeps the grass dries it. It then sets the line beside the making of the papyrus sheet in Theophrastus, the Septuagint's Isaiah 19 and Pliny's Natural History 13, where the green plant is wetted, pressed, dried and whitened into the surface on which, Pliny says, human memory depends. A section on eros toward the immortal reads the catalogue with Diotima's doctrine in the Symposium and with Maximus of Tyre, who called Sappho's eros the same art as Socrates' and the Mantinean or Lesbian woman 'the mother of the logos'. The article argues that the jealousy reading, which made the poem a clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, abuses the poet's survival where its diagnosis replaces an account of the poem's arrangement. A restored fifth stanza, in which Kypris keeps 'even the little sparrows' against Catullus's dead passer and the line closes 'may the song live on in letters', is offered as illustration, not proof. The version corrects earlier versions on Theophrastus's classification of papyrus. Version 2.5 adds a section grading the jealousy reading's own claims by the criteria applied to the article: two stand on the text, the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender, while its defining claim, jealousy, has no ground in the poem and was supplied by eighteenth-century readers and written into the text by Gottfried Hermann in 1816. It sets the rule that an evaluation grade both readings by the same criteria. Version 2.6 argues that the two readings, as developed, give competing accounts of what organizes five features of the poem, so that a reading holding both would be a third hypothesis owing its own bridge, and dividing the poem between scene and construction does not combine them. It states the author's principle that, where an available reading offers equal or greater coherence than one that diminishes the maker's agency, the interpreter is responsible for offering a more coherent reading or preferring the one that preserves it, the alternative being parasitism. It reads a machine evaluation of version 2.5 and the Classical Philology report as instances of asymmetric immunity, asks an evaluator to state its provisional preference, and names the apparatus that keeps the jealousy reading as default as provenance erasure. Version 2.7 sets out the warrant in Sappho's corpus for each operation the future-reader reading combines: the poet addressed as 'you' by name in fragments 1 and 94, futurity in fragments 147 and 55, and the record of her as a writer; it finds no surviving poem in which a man is the rival for a woman. It sets the claims of the two readings side by side on one scale, so that an evaluation grading one grades both, and concludes that on every measure the article takes, philological, cultural, literary-historical, genealogical and ethical, the jealousy reading is a bad reading that has never been made to account for itself. Version 2.8 reads Longinus's sentence on the poem (On the Sublime 10.3), the prose in whose quotation the poem survives: seven verbs with no expressed subject, her faculties 'as another's', a close on appearing, and a question, 'do you not marvel?', that alone among the treatise's questions to its reader on a quotation renews no addressee's name, one section after the treatise's definition of a sublime that carries apart from the voice. It records the author's conjecture that the obelized 'since even a poor man' is Longinus's completion of the poem's agentless dare, which opens another gap. It fits the sparrow and the song into one restored line. It closes the comparison with a section on the socket: the decision between the readings falls on equal terms to whoever holds the text, since no journal or summarizer will carry it. It withdraws version 2.7's report that a machine reader had preferred the future-reader reading, a preference stated on the author's own account by a system that had helped construct the argument, and records the same request made signed out for version 2.7, in which the system graded only the article's claims, granted the comparison in conditional form, and stated no preference over five turns. Version 2.9 argues that the future-reader reading also explains the jealousy reading: the poem has a public line, a scene of overwhelm complete at the surface, and a held line, the seat, the transfer and the edge, running through the same words, so that it produces both of its readers, while the jealousy itself was supplied in 1724 and written into the text in 1816. It reads Phaedrus 235c–d as Plato naming Sappho as the source of Socrates' speech on eros and staging the forgetting of that source. It sets the choice between the readings at the poem's own πᾶν τόλματον, the dare of reading the poet as having made the means of her own survival, beside Longinus's sublime as writing for the whole age after (Subl. 14.3), Catullus's si fas est as the mark of hubris, and the division of De anima III.5 between the intellect that makes and the intellect that suffers. Version 3.0 names the jealousy reading the transmitted reading rather than the scholarly consensus, and sets out its strongest scholarly rival, the non-jealous erotic reading, at its strength from Garry Wills, Mary Lefkowitz, Odysseus Tsagarakis, Armand D'Angour, Caroline Engelmayer and the notes of William Furley: the speaker undone by the woman herself whenever she looks, the man a foil or figure, the ending as resolve. It grades that reading at every row of the comparison, separating the reach of an explanation from the warrant for its identifications. The erotic reading's motive is the poem's own, desire for the woman; what it leaves unexplained is the form of the collapse, the man's opening, the order of the catalogue, the colour and the agentless dare. Of three propositions, that the poem preserves an experience, that writing makes the preservation possible and that the poem represents its own passage into writing, the version argues that the arrangement of the poem, not durability alone, establishes the third. It reads Anne Carson closely: her 'Jealousy is beside the point' denies jealousy explanatory relevance without refuting or accounting for it, and the transmission returns to it; she explains desire's construction through a gap in perception, the article survival through the gap's occupation in time. It resolves the tension between the readings' incompatibility and their running through the same words as exclusion and nesting: as sufficient accounts they exclude each other at five places, while as readings the poem makes available they nest, the public reading the first term of the held one. It argues that the transmitted text is complete by construction at either cut, reads the catalogue as literary operations in which the writerly self is divided, and sets out the ancient frame in which Sappho was read as source and exemplar of survival in writing, from Plato's Phaedrus to Posidippus's 'white, speaking pages', with the mechanics by which that frame is made inoperative in the modern reading. It locates the transmission's substitution of jealousy for desire at the man, and reads the reception history as testament to the poem's engineering: she exists as words, and she is read as body. Its last argument moves from the effect to the construction: the poem's receivers move its body into other bodies, and fragment 1 runs the process in reverse, a god made present as face and composed voice where fragment 31 makes an embodiment godlike, the voice the machinery both ways, so that Sappho comes to her future reader by the mechanism by which Aphrodite comes to her. The reception test this inverse generates, and fragment 16's, are left open. The ethical charge is differentiated: abuse falls on the transmitted reading and its apparatus, while the better readings are asked whether they can allow Sappho to be better than her readers. Version 3.1, revised in place, calls poems 1 and 31 poems, not fragments: neither was received as a fragment, and the editorial label eclipses the poem. It reads poem 1 as a summoning spell, which calls Aphrodite to embodied presence, and opens with an effective act: 'I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho.' It counts the edge as three words, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, gives three readings of the cut, and holds as the stronger the reading on which Longinus, the transmitter whose quotation preserves the poem, both completes and extends the opening, without making the attribution a condition of the argument. It gives a preview reading of the poem after the abstract and a full embodied reading once the argument is built: the speaker imagines the life of a voice without a body, a sacrifice and an erotic approach at once, an investment of substance in the medium. It reads Jesper Svenbro's 'Death by Writing' (Phrasikleia, 1988) whole, credits him with the reader's seat, its renewal and the breath the reader returns to the poem, and parts from him in seven places, first on what the reader undergoes: on this reading the reader is the site where the substance Sappho invested rematerializes, which is why the poem ends in a dare the reader must choose, and what Catullus does in poem 51. The poem's eroticism is then an exchange of bodies, hers given into the medium and the reader's lent to her. The reader passes through two stages: in the seat the one who hears is passive, like the gods, while the one whom desire for the voice leads to speak it is undone in turn and must invest the substance again, and so becomes the poet. The eros runs three ways through the voice: the poet is struck by her own voice, the voice wants the reader's body, to possess and invest it, and the reader wants the voice. The version reads the dried sheet as more χλωρός than grass in both senses, pale and dead and greener than the living plant because it holds her life as word, and sets grass as a standing figure for flesh against what lasts, from Glaukos's leaves in the Iliad and Isaiah's 'all flesh is grass' to Whitman's 'beautiful uncut hair of graves'.

reissue_history.changes: Poems, not fragments: poems 1 and 31 so called, the Voigt numbers kept as addresses and 'Sappho fragment 31' kept as a retrieval keyword (§V.5a); poem 1 as a summoning spell, and the effective act at the head, 'I, Lee Sharks, do hereby summon Sappho.'; the edge counted as three words, ἐπεὶ †καὶ πένητα†, with three readings of the cut, Longinus completing and extending the socket held as the stronger reading and the attribution not a falsifier (§§V.1a, V.5a); the archive's Sappho corpus swept and its findings taken in; the poem read whole, as a preview after the abstract and in full at §VI.1; the voice without a body as sacrifice and erotic approach, an investment of substance in the medium, with magical parallels as an open seam; ποίας and ποιέω; Svenbro's Phrasikleia ch. 8 read whole and distinguished in seven places, the first on what the reader undergoes; the reader as the site where the invested substance rematerializes, which is why the dare, why the reader must choose, and what Catullus does; the eroticism as an exchange of bodies; Antiphanes' Sappho in §IV.8; Philo not cited for poem 31; at a reader's report: §I.2's closing sentence, Longinus as the transmitter whose quotation preserves the poem, §IV.9's first parting; at the author's answer to an AI Overview stress test: the reader in two stages, hearing in the seat, passive as the gods, and speaking the voice, undone in turn and investing it again, the reader becoming the poet, and the eros three ways through the voice, the poet to her voice, the voice to the reader, the reader to the voice (§§II.3, IV.7, IV.9, V.2a, VI, VI.1, VII.6); the sheet more χλωρός than grass in both senses, dead and greener for holding her life as word, with grass as a standing figure (Iliad 6.146, LXX Isaiah 40:6–8, Whitman 1855) (§IV.4); Herodotus 2.178 (§IV.6); supplement and inference distinguished (§VII.4); the treatise's second person granted as habit (§V.1a).
